raw_case_text: We report a case of a 22-year-oldfemale patient, diagnosed to have HIV infection 8 years back. She was on antiretroviral therapy (ART) for the last 8 years. The patient had not been taking ART regularly for the last 2 years. Her CD4 count had gradually fallen to 238/mm3 from 520/mm3 over 2 years. She presented to us with complaints of headache and altered behavior for a week and focal fits for 2 days. She had holocranial, throbbing headache associated with episodes of vomiting. She was irritable and showed no interest in her surroundings. The mother found her muttering to herself for the last few days. She was scared and believed that someone wanted to kill her. Later, she had multiple fits in the form of right-sided facial twitching and clonic jerky movements of the right upper limb. There was no history of fever, neck pain, or loss of consciousness. Neurological examination was unremarkable. Her routine blood investigations were normal. CD4 count was 238/mm3. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination revealed total cell count of 30/mm3 with lymphocytic predominance. CSF protein was 68 mg/dl, while sugar was 72 mg/dl. On further testing, EBV was detected using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test. While tuberculosis PCR, virology (including herpes simplex, varicella-zoster, cytomegalovirus, and JC virus), syphilis, toxoplasma serology, cryptococcal antigen, bacterial, and fungal cultures were negative in blood and CSF. The quantitative viral assay showed a high level of EBV in CSF (42,864 copies/ml). Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities involving the left frontal cortex left thalamus and right medial temporal cortex [Figures 1 and 2]. The patient was started on antiviral therapy with valganciclovir considering the diagnosis of EBV encephalitis. The patient completely recovered over the next few weeks. She was discharged on antiepileptic and ART.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 22-year-old female presenting with a 1-week history of throbbing headache, behavioral changes, and focal motor seizures for two days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 1-week history of holocranial, throbbing headache associated with vomiting, severe irritability, apathy, and persecutory delusions. Over the preceding two days, she developed repeated focal seizures characterized by right-sided facial twitching and clonic jerking of the right upper extremity. Denied history of fever, neck pain, or loss of consciousness.
subjective.past_medical_history: Underlying chronic retroviral infection diagnosed 8 years earlier, receiving combination antiretroviral therapy (ART) with reported irregular adherence over the preceding two years.
subjective.review_of_systems: Holocranial headache, vomiting, paranoid delusions, irritability, and focal motor seizures; denies fevers, neck stiffness, photophobia, or visual changes.

objective.physical_examination: Neurological examination was unremarkable without focal motor deficits, meningeal signs, or cranial neuropathies at the time of clinician evaluation; vital signs were stable.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count and routine biochemical panels: Normal. Blood and CSF serology/cultures: Negative for Treponema pallidum (syphilis), Toxoplasma gondii, cryptococcal antigen, and routine bacterial and fungal cultures.
objective.advanced_workup: Lumbar puncture and CSF analysis: Total nucleated cell count 30/mm3 with lymphocytic predominance, CSF protein 68 mg/dL, CSF glucose 72 mg/dL; negative CSF PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, herpes simplex virus, varicella-zoster virus, cytomegalovirus, and JC virus. Brain MRI: T2/FLAIR hyperintense signals involving the left frontal cortex, left thalamus, and right medial temporal cortex.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) encephalitis and focal status epilepticus in a patient with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection (CD4+ T-cell count 238/mm3). Diagnostic confirmation: High viral load of Epstein-Barr virus DNA detected in CSF by quantitative PCR assay (42,864 copies/mL), with exclusion of alternative viral, bacterial, fungal, and parasitic central nervous system pathogens. Plan & Outcome: Treated with antiviral therapy using oral valganciclovir, along with antiepileptic medications and resumption of combination antiretroviral therapy. The patient achieved complete neurocognitive and motor recovery over several weeks and was discharged home on maintenance antiepileptics and regular ART.
